question: Two teams of horsemen fight over the headless carcass of a goat, dragging it around a marker and back into a scoring circle, in matches that can last for hours. Buzkashi is the national sport of which country?

options.info: Traditionally played on the northern plains, it was banned under the first Taliban government and revived afterwards; top riders are sponsored by wealthy patrons.
Plays its own related horseback game, kokpar, but the sport's name and national status belong elsewhere.
Hosts the World Nomad Games and plays kok-boru, a cousin of this sport with a proper goal-shaped scoring pit.
Famous for its Akhal-Teke horses, prized for endurance and a metallic sheen, but not for this game.

question: In 2018 a nation of barely four million people played three consecutive extra-time knockout matches, then beat England in the semi-final before losing the World Cup final in Moscow. Which country?

options.info: Luka Modrić won the Golden Ball; the team lost 4-2 to France in the final and finished third four years later.
Its 'golden generation' finished third at the same tournament, beating England in the play-off.
Won the 1992 European Championship after being called up as a late replacement, but went out in the last 16 in 2018.
Reached the quarter-finals in 2018, where it was knocked out by the eventual runners-up.

question: A record that had stood since 1984 finally fell in February 2023, when a player who entered the league straight out of high school in 2003 passed 38,388 career regular-season points. Who is now the NBA's all-time leading scorer?

options.info: He broke the record in his 20th season, having never missed the playoffs in his prime years, and later played in the same team as his own son.
Held the record for nearly four decades thanks largely to his unblockable skyhook.
Retired with six championships and the highest career points-per-game average, but fewer total points.
Spent 18 seasons in Utah and sits second on the all-time scoring list without ever winning a title.

question: Roughly 1,500 kilometres of frozen river, mountain pass and sea ice, run every March by teams of dogs and a single musher, commemorating a 1925 emergency serum run to a diphtheria-stricken town. In which US state is the Iditarod run?

options.info: The route runs from Anchorage to Nome; the serum relay it honours is also why a statue of the lead dog Balto stands in New York's Central Park.
Hosts the John Beargrease Sled Dog Marathon, a serious race but a much shorter one.
Has a long-distance sled dog race of its own, though not this one.
Runs the Can-Am Crown sled dog races in the far north of the state, on a far smaller scale.

question: This club won the first five editions of Europe's top club football competition in the 1950s and has kept adding to the tally ever since, holding a lead no rival has come close to closing. Which club has won the European Cup and Champions League most often?

options.info: Its total is well into double figures, roughly twice that of its nearest challenger, and includes a run of three consecutive titles from 2016 to 2018.
Europe's second most successful club in the competition, with seven titles.
England's most successful club in the tournament, including the 2005 comeback from 3-0 down in Istanbul.
Germany's dominant force, with six European titles including a treble-winning 2020.

question: At the 1968 Mexico City Olympics one high jumper ignored a century of straddle and scissors technique, sprinted at the bar in a curve and went over backwards, head first. Within a decade almost every serious jumper in the world had copied him. Who was he?

options.info: The 'Fosbury flop' only became safe once foam landing pits replaced sand and sawdust; he won gold with an Olympic record of 2.24 m.
The Soviet world record holder of the early 1960s, and a master of the older straddle technique this jumper replaced.
The Cuban who set the current world record of 2.45 m in 1993, using the technique invented here.
Also made history at the same 1968 Games, but with a long jump so far it broke the measuring equipment.

question: In the mid-1970s a Chilean-French director assembled Salvador Dalí, Orson Welles, Mick Jagger, Pink Floyd and the artist H.R. Giger for a science-fiction epic he estimated would run fourteen hours. No studio would fund it, but the storyboards leaked into the visual language of half of 1980s cinema. Whose unmade 'Dune' was it?

options.info: His enormous illustrated production bible circulated in Hollywood for years; the 2013 documentary 'Jodorowsky's Dune' tells the story.
Was genuinely attached to a 'Dune' adaptation for a while after this attempt collapsed, before leaving to make 'Blade Runner'.
Actually did direct a 'Dune' film, released in 1984, and spent decades disowning it.
Has his own legendary tale of a doomed production, having spent nearly thirty years trying to film Don Quixote.

question: The Academy only created a competitive award for animated features in 2001, after years of animated films being shut out of the main race. Which film won it first?

options.info: DreamWorks' fairy-tale satire beat two other nominees in the inaugural year, one of which was Pixar's 'Monsters, Inc.'.
Nominated in that first year and lost; Pixar would go on to dominate the category later.
Won the award the following year, becoming the first hand-drawn and first non-English winner.
Released in 1999, before the category existed at all; it took a Golden Globe instead.

question: A former paratrooper turned television writer grew so tired of network censors softening his scripts about racism and politics that he moved the arguments to other planets and the far future, then introduced each episode himself in a narrow suit and clipped voice. Who created 'The Twilight Zone'?

options.info: He wrote roughly half the show's episodes himself and became one of the most recognisable on-screen hosts in television history.
Used a similar trick a few years later, smuggling social commentary into 'Star Trek'.
Wrote some of the series' most famous episodes, including the one with the gremlin on the aeroplane wing, but did not create it.
Contributed a script and was an obvious influence, though the show was not his.

question: Spanning fifty years from the warlord era through the Japanese occupation to the Cultural Revolution, and following two Peking opera performers bound together since childhood training, this 1993 epic became the first Chinese film to win the Palme d'Or at Cannes. Who directed 'Farewell My Concubine'?

options.info: A leading figure of China's Fifth Generation; the film was briefly banned at home before being allowed a censored release.
His classmate and the cinematographer on Chen's debut, later famous for 'Raise the Red Lantern' and 'Hero'.
A Hong Kong stylist who won Best Director at Cannes for 'Happy Together', a very different kind of film.
Defined the Hong Kong action film before moving to Hollywood; not an arthouse Cannes winner.

question: Famous for staying in character between takes and for retiring from acting more than once, including a spell learning shoemaking in Italy, this actor holds the record for the most Best Actor Oscars, with three. Who?

options.info: He won for 'My Left Foot', 'There Will Be Blood' and 'Lincoln', and announced his retirement after 'Phantom Thread'.
Has three acting Oscars too, but one of them is for a supporting role, leaving him on two in this category.
Won twice and famously sent an activist to decline the second on his behalf.
Won back-to-back Best Actor awards in 1994 and 1995, a rare feat, but has not added a third.

question: The producers wanted Cary Grant but knew he would only sign for one picture, so they gambled on a Scottish former milkman and bodybuilder who had once competed in a Mr Universe contest. Who introduced himself as Bond in the 1962 film 'Dr. No'?

options.info: Ian Fleming initially thought him wrong for the part, then wrote Scottish ancestry into the character after seeing the film.
An Australian model who took over for a single film, 'On Her Majesty's Secret Service', in 1969.
Played the role seven times from 1973, in a lighter, more comic register.
Was Fleming's own preferred choice and did play a version of the character, but only in the 1967 spoof 'Casino Royale'.

question: Listen to the clip below. This piano movement sits third in a four-part suite named after a region of northern Italy, and its composer disliked being called an Impressionist even as the label stuck to him for good. Who wrote it?

audio.credit: Performed by Laurens Goedhart — CC BY 3.0 recording via Wikimedia Commons

options.info: 'Clair de lune' comes from his 'Suite bergamasque', begun around 1890 but not published until 1905, by which time he had moved on stylistically.
Also set a poem called 'Clair de lune' by the same poet, Verlaine, which is a common source of confusion.
A Belgian-French composer of the previous generation, known for organ works and a single monumental symphony.
A French composer of colourful orchestral pieces such as 'España', but not this one.

question: Listen to the clip below — a tone poem in which a solo violin, deliberately mistuned, plays Death calling skeletons out of their graves to dance until the oboe imitates a cockerel at dawn. Which French composer wrote it?

audio.credit: Philadelphia Symphony Orchestra conducted by Leopold Stokowski, early Victor recording — public domain via Wikimedia Commons

options.info: 'Danse macabre' shocked audiences in 1874 with its xylophone rattling like bones; he reused the theme in 'The Carnival of the Animals'.
Wrote his own witches' sabbath finale in the 'Symphonie fantastique', which quotes the same Dies irae chant, but this is not his.
Composer of 'The Sorcerer's Apprentice', another French orchestral showpiece built on a supernatural story.
A contemporary best known for operas such as 'Manon' and the 'Méditation' from 'Thaïs'.

question: Watch the clip below. Written by a band of Los Angeles session musicians who had never set foot on the continent they were singing about, this 1982 track was almost left off the album, then became the group's only US number one — and decades later was voted back into the charts by the internet. Which band?

audio.credit: Toto – 'Africa' official video, via TotoVEVO on YouTube

options.info: 'Africa' reached number one in 1983; its players had already backed everyone from Steely Dan to Michael Jackson as studio musicians.
Another American band built around slick musicianship and horns, with a very different catalogue of ballads.
A transatlantic rock band of the same era whose biggest hit was 'I Want to Know What Love Is'.
American arena rockers active in exactly the same years, but not the makers of this record.

question: Watch this vintage swing-style cover, recorded live in one take. The song it reworks was released in 1981, opens with a piano riff and a small-town girl on a midnight train, and was resurrected in 2007 by the final scene of a famous mob drama. Which band recorded the original?

audio.credit: Cover: Postmodern Jukebox – 'Don't Stop Believin'' one-take vintage cover, via PostmodernJukebox on YouTube — original song by Journey

options.info: Steve Perry's vocal on 'Don't Stop Believin'' made it one of the best-selling digital tracks of a song recorded before the download era.
A contemporary rock band with a similarly huge radio presence, but not the writers of this song.
Topped the charts in 1981 with 'Keep On Loving You', from the same corner of American rock.
Another arena-rock act of the era, remembered for 'Mr. Roboto' and 'Come Sail Away'.

question: In 1965 a trade paper ran an advert seeking 'four insane boys' for a television series. Out of 400-odd hopefuls, four were cast to play a struggling pop group — and then the fictional group started outselling real ones, eventually fighting the producers for the right to play their own instruments. Which band?

options.info: Micky Dolenz, Davy Jones, Michael Nesmith and Peter Tork were assembled by casting call; their 1967 album sales reportedly beat the Beatles and the Rolling Stones combined that year.
A later television musical family, but its records were mostly studio productions with no such revolt.
Existed only as cartoon characters, with session singers behind 'Sugar, Sugar' — nobody was cast to appear on screen.
A costumed animal band from a children's variety show of the same era, never intended as a chart act.

question: An abbess in the Rhineland who reported visions from childhood, wrote medical and botanical treatises, corresponded with emperors and popes, and composed a body of soaring monophonic chant plus what may be the earliest surviving morality play set to music. Who was this 12th-century figure?

options.info: Her chants, collected as the 'Symphonia', enjoyed a huge revival on recordings from the 1980s; she was declared a Doctor of the Church in 2012.
A Venetian singer and composer of the 1600s who published more secular vocal music in her lifetime than most of her male contemporaries.
A 14th-century French poet-composer, central to the Ars nova and to early polyphonic mass settings.
A composer at Notre-Dame in Paris around 1200, known for expanding chant into three and four voices.

question: In August 1942, in a city under siege and starving, a symphony was performed by an orchestra so depleted that army musicians were pulled from the front line to fill the seats, and loudspeakers broadcast it towards the enemy trenches. Who wrote this Seventh Symphony?

options.info: He began the 'Leningrad' Symphony in the besieged city while serving as a volunteer fire warden, and the score was flown out on microfilm to be played worldwide.
Was evacuated from Moscow during the same war and wrote a wartime epic of his own, the opera 'War and Peace'.
An Armenian-Soviet composer whose 'Sabre Dance' and ballet scores made him internationally famous in the same decade.
Finland's national composer, who had stopped publishing new work entirely by this point.

question: In October 2018 a framed canvas sold at Sotheby's for over a million pounds, and the moment the hammer fell an alarm sounded and the picture slid halfway through a shredder hidden in its own frame. The half-destroyed work was later resold for many times the price. Which artist built the frame?

options.info: The work, 'Girl with Balloon', was renamed 'Love Is in the Bin'; the artist said the shredder was meant to destroy it completely but jammed halfway.
Britain's other great art-market provocateur, known for a diamond-encrusted skull and for pickled sharks.
Taped a banana to a wall at an art fair in 2019, a comparable stunt but a different one.
Makes mirror-polished balloon animals at monumental scale, and holds auction records of his own.

question: For centuries it was assumed to be a night scene, until a 1940s cleaning stripped away darkened varnish and revealed broad daylight. The huge militia group portrait is also missing strips cut off all four sides in 1715 so it would fit a wall in Amsterdam's town hall. Who painted 'The Night Watch'?

options.info: He broke with the flat, evenly lit convention of group portraits by staging the company as if bursting into motion; the painting now hangs in the Rijksmuseum.
The other great Dutch painter of militia banquets, working in Haarlem with far looser brushwork.
Painted small, silent domestic interiors and left only around 35 known works, none of them group portraits.
A Flemish master of the same century, running a huge Antwerp workshop devoted to mythological and religious scenes.

question: The daughter of a famous poet, she worked on notes for an unbuilt mechanical calculating engine in the 1840s and appended a method for computing Bernoulli numbers with it — plus a remark that such a machine might one day compose music. Who was she?

options.info: Byron's daughter, she annotated Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine; her Note G is often called the first published computer program.
A US Navy officer who built the first compiler a century later and popularised the term 'debugging'.
A Scottish science writer of the same era who actually tutored the correct answer in mathematics.
A Hollywood star who co-patented a frequency-hopping system now credited as a forerunner of wireless communication.

question: Convinced that stomach ulcers were caused by bacteria rather than stress and spicy food, and unable to persuade anyone, an Australian doctor in 1984 drank a beaker of the bug himself, got violently ill, and proved his point with his own biopsy. Who was he?

options.info: He and pathologist Robin Warren shared the 2005 Nobel Prize for identifying Helicobacter pylori; ulcers are now routinely cured with antibiotics.
Another famous self-experimenter — he threaded a catheter into his own heart in 1929 — but in a completely different field.
Pioneered chemotherapy and the idea of a 'magic bullet' drug, decades earlier.
An Australian pharmacologist too, but his Nobel was for turning penicillin into a usable medicine.

question: During a solar eclipse in 1868, astronomers saw a yellow spectral line that matched no element known on Earth, and named the new substance after the Greek word for the sun. It was another 27 years before anyone found it in the ground. Which element?

options.info: Named from 'helios'; it was finally isolated on Earth in 1895 from a uranium mineral, and today's supply comes mostly from natural gas fields.
Dominates the Sun by mass, but had already been identified in a laboratory in the 1760s.
Its name does come from Greek, but it was found on Earth first, in liquefied air in 1898.
Isolated from air in 1894 by Rayleigh and Ramsay, not from sunlight.

question: On a long boat journey from Madras to England in 1930, a nineteen-year-old worked out that a dying star above a certain mass cannot settle into a white dwarf and must collapse further. A senior astronomer publicly ridiculed the idea for years; the Nobel Prize arrived in 1983. Whose limit is it?

options.info: The limit is about 1.4 solar masses; NASA later named its X-ray space observatory after him.
The eminent astrophysicist who dismissed the calculation at a 1935 meeting, setting the theory back by decades.
Explained how heavy elements are forged in stars, and coined the term 'Big Bang' as a jibe.
A Belgian priest and physicist who proposed the expanding universe model, a different corner of astrophysics.

question: Half a millimetre long, eight-legged and vaguely resembling a bear, these animals can dry out into a glassy 'tun' state, survive boiling, freezing near absolute zero, huge radiation doses and even open space — then rehydrate and walk away. What are they?

options.info: Also called water bears or moss piglets, they were sent into orbit in 2007 and survived direct exposure to vacuum and solar radiation.
Microscopic animals that also survive drying out, and one group has famously reproduced without sex for millions of years.
Roundworms found nearly everywhere on Earth, some of which can also enter dormancy, but not the animals described here.
Sold as 'sea monkeys' because their eggs survive long drying, but adults are far less durable.

question: Cosmic rays constantly create a rare, unstable form of an element in the upper atmosphere, living things absorb it while alive and stop when they die, and it halves in quantity roughly every 5,700 years — which is why archaeologists can date a wooden beam or a bone. Which isotope?

options.info: Willard Libby developed the dating method in the late 1940s and won a Nobel Prize; it is useful back to around 50,000 years.
The ordinary, stable form of carbon — it never decays, so it carries no clock.
Genuinely used for dating, but with a half-life over a billion years, so it suits volcanic rock rather than organic remains.
Used to date the oldest rocks and meteorites, on timescales of billions of years.

question: This country contains roughly twice as many ancient pyramids as its more famous northern neighbour — several hundred of them, steeper, smaller and built for the rulers of Kush at sites like Meroë. Which country?

options.info: The Kushite kings even ruled Egypt for a time as its 25th Dynasty; many Meroë pyramids had their tops blasted off by a 19th-century treasure hunter.
Has spectacular Greek and Roman ruins such as Leptis Magna, but no pyramid fields.
Home to the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela and the stelae of Axum, but not pyramids.
Holds remarkable prehistoric rock art in the Ennedi massif, again a different kind of monument.

question: Sitting in a rift valley in southern Siberia, it plunges over 1,600 metres and holds roughly a fifth of all the unfrozen fresh water on the planet — more than all five North American Great Lakes combined. Which lake?

options.info: About 25 million years old, it is home to the world's only exclusively freshwater seal, the nerpa, and freezes over thickly enough to drive on.
The world's second deepest and second largest by volume, in the East African Rift.
The largest inland body of water by area, but far shallower relative to its size and salty in most parts.
The largest freshwater lake by surface area, though it holds only a fraction of this lake's volume.

question: Its king declared in the 1970s that a certain index mattered more than gross domestic product, television was only legalised in 1999, and its forests absorb more carbon than the country emits. Which Himalayan kingdom measures Gross National Happiness?

options.info: The constitution requires at least 60% forest cover; tourism is deliberately limited by a daily sustainable development fee.
Its own monarchy was abolished in 2008, and it pursues conventional development indicators.
Was an independent Himalayan kingdom until 1975, when it became an Indian state — a real place, but not a country today.
A landlocked Southeast Asian republic, mountainous but nowhere near the Himalayas.

question: Encircled by Nationalist forces in the south, roughly 86,000 Communist troops broke out in October 1934 and walked, fought and starved their way some 9,000 kilometres north over a year; barely a tenth arrived, but the survivor who emerged in charge led the country for the next four decades. What is this retreat called?

options.info: It confirmed Mao Zedong's leadership of the party and became the founding legend of the People's Republic, including the crossing of the Luding bridge.
A disastrous industrialisation and collectivisation campaign of 1958-62, decades later and not a military retreat.
An anti-foreign uprising around 1900, crushed by an eight-nation alliance.
A real campaign of 1926-28, but a Nationalist offensive against warlords rather than a Communist retreat.

question: A single sandstone dome rising over 300 metres from flat desert, sacred to the Anangu people, formally handed back to them in 1985 and closed to climbers in 2019. What is this monolith in Australia's Northern Territory called?

options.info: Officially dual-named Uluru / Ayers Rock; most of its bulk is thought to continue several kilometres underground.
The cluster of 36 domed rocks about 25 kilometres away, in the same national park.
A rock in Western Australia often claimed to be larger, though it is a different kind of formation.
A curling granite cliff in Western Australia, striking but far smaller.

question: For a brief window in the 1970s this 21-square-kilometre Pacific republic had close to the highest income per person on Earth, thanks to a plateau of phosphate rock left by seabirds. The rock ran out, the money was lost in bad investments, and today most of the interior is unusable mined-out pinnacles. Which country?

options.info: The world's smallest island republic; it later took income from hosting an Australian offshore detention centre.
Another tiny Pacific state, but its unexpected windfall came from leasing its '.tv' internet domain.
Spread across a vast area of ocean; its own phosphate island, Banaba, was mined out under British administration.
A Micronesian republic whose economy rests on diving tourism and a US compact, not phosphate.

question: Having escaped slavery in Maryland in 1849, she returned south around thirteen times to guide roughly seventy people out, later scouted for the Union army and led an armed raid that freed hundreds. Who was she?

options.info: Nicknamed 'Moses', she was the first woman to lead an armed US military expedition, the 1863 Combahee River raid.
A formerly enslaved preacher and abolitionist orator, famous for a speech on women's rights, but not a conductor on the escape network.
The era's most prominent Black abolitionist writer and speaker, who knew and praised the correct answer.
A journalist who documented lynching in the 1890s, a generation later.

question: In 1803 a cash-strapped Napoleon offered far more than the port city the American envoys had been sent to buy, and for about 15 million dollars the young United States doubled in size at roughly three cents an acre. What was this deal called?

options.info: It added all or part of fifteen future states; Jefferson privately doubted the constitution allowed him to do it, and did it anyway.
A separate deal, buying Russian territory in 1867 and mocked at the time as 'Seward's Folly'.
A much smaller 1853 strip bought from Mexico to allow a southern railway route.
Spain gave up Florida in the 1819 Adams-Onís Treaty, a genuine transfer but a fraction of the size.

question: Born into a wealthy Caracas family, he crossed the flooded plains and a 4,000-metre Andean pass with an exhausted army to surprise the Spanish at Boyacá in 1819, and gave his name to a country he never managed to keep united. Who was he?

options.info: His Gran Colombia broke apart within a decade; Bolivia is named after him, and he died disillusioned in 1830.
Liberated the southern half of the continent and met the correct answer at Guayaquil in 1822, then withdrew from politics entirely.
A leader of Chilean independence, of Irish descent, who fought alongside San Martín.
The correct answer's most trusted general, who won the decisive battle of Ayacucho and became Bolivia's first elected president.

question: Soviet planners diverted two rivers to irrigate cotton fields from the 1960s, and what had been one of the four largest lakes on Earth shrank to a fraction of its area, stranding rusting fishing boats dozens of kilometres from any water. Which body of water?

options.info: Split between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan; a dam has partially restored the northern lobe, while the southern part is largely a salt desert.
Has also shrunk dramatically, but mainly through drought and climate change rather than a single irrigation scheme.
An Iranian salt lake that shrank severely for similar reasons, on a smaller scale.
A shrinking, hypersaline Californian lake created by accident in 1905 when irrigation works failed.

question: Between November 1884 and February 1885, fourteen powers met around a table to agree the rules for claiming territory on a continent where not one African representative was present. What is this meeting usually called?

options.info: Convened by Bismarck, it set the 'effective occupation' principle and formalised the scramble that produced today's often arbitrary borders.
Redrew Europe after Napoleon in 1814-15, seventy years earlier and about a different continent.
Split the newly encountered world between Spain and Portugal in 1494, an equally sweeping but far older division.
A real 1889-90 meeting on the slave trade in the same region, but not the one that carved up the map.

question: French soldiers rebuilding a fort near a Nile Delta town in 1799 dug out a slab carrying the same decree in three scripts — and because scholars could already read one of them, the other two finally became legible. What is this slab called?

options.info: Surrendered to the British in 1801 and in the British Museum ever since; Jean-François Champollion announced his decipherment of the hieroglyphs in 1822.
A trilingual cliff carving in Iran that played the equivalent role for cuneiform.
A ceremonial Egyptian slate from around 3100 BC showing a king, but carrying no bilingual text.
A genuine fragment of Egyptian royal annals, valuable for chronology but not a key to the script.

question: A 19th-century excavator noticed odd cavities in the hardened ash and had the idea of pumping plaster into them, producing casts of people and a dog in the postures in which they died in AD 79. In which buried town was this technique developed?

options.info: Giuseppe Fiorelli introduced the plaster casting method in the 1860s; the town was buried under metres of pumice and ash.
Destroyed by the same eruption, but by hot surges that carbonised wood and left skeletons rather than these voids.
Rome's port town, abandoned gradually over centuries and never buried by an eruption.
A third settlement hit in AD 79, known for its seaside villas rather than for this discovery.

question: At a supermarket in Troy, Ohio, in June 1974, a cashier passed the first ever retail item across a laser scanner. The product was chosen partly because it was small enough to prove the stripes could be printed on something tiny. What was it?

options.text: A ten-pack of Wrigley's chewing gum
options.info: It cost 67 cents, and the pack is now in the Smithsonian; the code itself had been sketched out decades earlier in beach sand.
An obvious guess given the brand's fame in American retail history, but not the first scan.

options.text: A box of Kellogg's Corn Flakes
options.info: Cereal boxes were among the first products widely coded, but this was not the item at the till that morning.
A famously early adopter of packaging innovations, though not involved in this particular first.

question: The best-supported account traces the world's most widely understood two-letter expression to a short-lived Boston newspaper fad of 1839 for jokey abbreviations of deliberately misspelled phrases, boosted a year later by a presidential campaign club. What was 'OK' originally short for?

options.text: 'Oll korrect', a joke misspelling of 'all correct'
options.info: It survived because Martin Van Buren's 1840 re-election campaign adopted it for 'Old Kinderhook', his New York birthplace.
A popular story, but the expression is documented in print well before the American Civil War.

options.text: 'Aux Cayes', a Haitian port known for good rum
options.info: One of many folk etymologies proposed over the years, without documentary support.
Another appealing theory, but there is no evidence connecting it to the American origin of the term.

question: In 1900 there were around 3,000 cars in France, and two brothers gave away a free handbook listing mechanics, petrol sellers and places to eat — the point being to make people drive further and wear out more of their product. Which company's guide became the world's most feared restaurant rating?

options.info: The tyre makers began charging for the guide in 1920 and introduced the star system in the 1920s and 30s; inspectors still dine anonymously.
A French manufacturer of the same era that made bicycles and cars, but never a restaurant guide.
Did publish motoring and county guides for drivers in Britain, though without the starred restaurant ratings.
Founded later and famous for advertising stunts such as lighting up the Eiffel Tower, not for gastronomy.

question: In 1912 an American pharmacist devised the scale still used to rank chilli heat, running from zero for a bell pepper into the millions for the fiercest cultivars. How did his original method actually measure the heat?

options.text: A panel of tasters diluted the extract in sugar water until nobody could detect any burn
options.info: The dilution factor became the rating, which is why early figures were rounded and subjective; modern labs use liquid chromatography instead.

options.text: The extract was burned and the smoke analysed for capsaicin
options.info: Capsaicin is measured chemically today, but by chromatography rather than combustion.

options.text: Chillies were weighed before and after drying, with heat inferred from moisture loss
options.info: Drying does concentrate flavour, but it tells you nothing about pungency.

options.text: A drop of extract was applied to the skin and the reddening measured
options.info: Capsaicin does irritate skin, and appears in warming ointments, but that was never the basis of the scale.

question: Think of a wheat field in late August, the ears heavy and ready for the harvester, and the precious metal that colour is forever compared to. Those two things, one after the other, spell the surname of the Viennese prodigy who was writing acclaimed operas in his twenties and later won an Oscar for scoring 'The Adventures of Robin Hood'. Who was he?

options.info: Mahler called him a genius as a boy; exile from Nazi Austria pushed him into Hollywood, where he essentially invented the lush symphonic film score.
Another Viennese émigré who scored 'King Kong' and 'Gone with the Wind' — and whose surname likewise hides a very ordinary building material.
A German-born Hollywood composer of 'Sunset Boulevard', whose original surname, Wachsmann, points to a substance candles are made of.
A Hungarian composer of Hollywood epics such as 'Ben-Hur', with a surname that is not German at all.

question: Every spring, German bakery and chocolate-shop windows fill with figures of the long-eared creature that supposedly hides the Easter eggs. Double the 's' in that animal's name and you have the surname of the Dresden court composer whose Italian operas rivalled Handel's in 1730s London. Who was he?

options.info: Enormously famous in his lifetime and married to the star soprano Faustina Bordoni, he wrote more than 60 operas and was then almost entirely forgotten.
A prolific Hamburg opera composer of the same era, with a surname a single letter away from an imperial title.
Frederick the Great's court composer in Berlin, best known for the passion oratorio 'Der Tod Jesu'.
A Hamburg composer and writer who once fought a duel with Handel over an organ bench, but not the man described here.

question: At a village festival in Vorarlberg the brass band announces its next piece as 'ein zünftiger Marsch' and everyone starts stamping in time. Add three letters to the end of that piece's name and you have the surname of the German Romantic who wrote the vampire opera 'Der Vampyr' and 'Hans Heiling'. Who was he?

options.info: The main link between Weber's supernatural romanticism and Wagner's early operas; 'Der Vampyr' premiered in 1828, seventy years before Dracula.
A composer of the same generation, remembered for 'Das Nachtlager in Granada', whose surname carries a rather ecclesiastical shape.
The great man of German comic opera, with 'Zar und Zimmermann' and 'Der Wildschütz'.
A violin virtuoso and composer who wrote his own supernatural opera, 'Faust', and invented the chin rest.

question: Opera houses and concert halls in German-speaking countries print 'Uraufführung' in bold on a poster, and it is treated as a far bigger event than an 'Erstaufführung' of the same piece. What does it announce?

options.text: The very first public performance of the work anywhere in the world
options.info: Houses compete fiercely for them; an 'Erstaufführung' is merely the first time that city or country has heard the piece.

options.text: The first performance of a work in a newly revised version by the composer
options.info: Revised versions do get announced, but with wording like 'Neufassung' rather than this term.

options.text: The opening night of a run after the dress rehearsal
options.info: That is simply the Premiere for that production, which may be of a centuries-old work.

options.text: A performance using the composer's original manuscript rather than a later edition
options.info: That idea exists in the concert world, but it travels under the label 'Urtext' instead.

question: You leave a party, and only once you are already on your way down from the flat does the perfect crushing reply finally arrive — far too late to use. German has a compound noun for exactly that joke. What does 'Treppenwitz' literally picture?

options.text: A joke that arrives on the staircase
options.info: The image is of the retort occurring to you as you head down the stairs; French has the same idea as 'l'esprit de l'escalier'.

options.text: A joke told at someone else's expense
options.info: German would reach for something like 'Spott' for that, not this compound.

options.text: A joke that builds step by step to its punchline
options.info: A tempting reading of the first half, but the steps here are literal ones you are walking down.
Evocative, but the word describes bad timing rather than a bad joke.

question: Your partner is twenty minutes late and not answering the phone, and by minute twenty-five you have already pictured the ambulance, the hospital corridor and the funeral. German speakers describe that runaway private film with the word 'Kopfkino'. What is the image behind it?

options.info: The compound puts a picture house behind your forehead — used for anything from anxious catastrophising to daydreams you would rather not describe out loud.

options.text: A headache brought on by too much screen time
options.info: A modern-sounding guess, but the second half of the word is a place, not a pain.

options.text: A memory you cannot stop replaying
options.info: Close in feeling, though the German word is about scenes you invent rather than ones you lived.

options.text: Talking yourself through a task in your head
options.info: That inner monologue is a real phenomenon, but German does not name it with this compound.
